page_header: Chemical Equilibrium, Acids and Bases · 4 marks

steps.label: Lewis acid
lines: Lewis acid: a substance that can accept a
lone pair of electrons.
Example: BF₃ (the boron atom has only six
valence electrons, so it can accept a lone
pair).
steps.why: The Lewis theory defines acid and base by electron pairs, not by protons. Acceptor of a lone pair is the whole definition, and BF₃ is the standard example because boron's octet is incomplete.
common_mistakes: Writing proton donor. That is the Brønsted-Lowry acid, not the Lewis acid.
Writing electron acceptor without the word pair. The acid accepts a lone PAIR of electrons.
steps.memory_tip: Acid Accepts the pair — both words start with A.
steps.margin_note: Electron-pair acceptor, never proton donor — the theories must not mix.

steps.label: Types of Lewis acids
lines: a) Simple cations: Ag⁺, Co³⁺
b) Molecules whose central atom has an
incomplete octet: BF₃, BCl₃
c) Molecules with multiple bonds between
atoms of different electronegativity:
CO₂, SO₂
steps.why: Each type is a different reason the substance can take a lone pair: a positive charge, an empty place in the octet, or a multiple bond whose electrons are pulled away from the central atom. Type (c) must be written with its full wording. The multiple bond has to join atoms of DIFFERENT electronegativity, so the bonding electrons are pulled towards the more electronegative atom — the oxygen in CO₂ and SO₂ — and the central atom is left with a place to accept a pair. The words multiple bonds appear again in the Lewis base list one step below, for CO and NO, and they are not the same test there. The test that decides is the lone pair: a molecule is a Lewis acid if it has a place to TAKE a pair, and a Lewis base if it has a lone pair to GIVE. Check for the lone pair first, not for the bond.
common_mistakes: Listing anions such as Cl⁻ as Lewis acids. Anions hold extra electrons, so they are bases.

Shortening type (c) to molecules with multiple bonds. The Lewis base list uses those same words for CO and NO. The acid type needs the full wording: a multiple bond between atoms of different electronegativity.
Giving the types without one example each. The examples carry the mark with the list.
steps.memory_tip: Three ways to have room for a pair: positive charge, empty octet, shiftable multiple bond.
steps.margin_note: Three labelled types, one example each. Write type (c) in full: the multiple bond is between atoms of DIFFERENT electronegativity.

steps.label: Lewis base and its types
lines: Lewis base: a substance that can donate a
lone pair of electrons.
a) Simple anions: Cl⁻, OH⁻
b) Molecules with lone pairs on the central
atom: H₂O, NH₃
c) Molecules with multiple bonds: CO, NO
steps.why: The base is the opposite of the acid: it has a lone pair available and donates it into the new bond. The list covers three ways of having a spare pair — a negative charge (anions), a lone pair on the central atom (H₂O, NH₃), and the book's third group, molecules with multiple bonds (CO, NO). Read that third group carefully, because the words repeat in the acid list two steps above. CO and NO donate the lone pair that sits on the carbon or the nitrogen atom; the multiple bond itself is not what they give away. In CO₂ and SO₂ the multiple bond joins atoms of different electronegativity, its electrons shift towards oxygen, and that leaves the central atom able to ACCEPT a pair — which is why those molecules are Lewis acids. So the same phrase names an acid in one list and a base in the other. The deciding test is not the bond: it is whether the molecule has a lone pair to give (base) or a place to take one (acid).
common_mistakes: Writing proton acceptor. That is the Brønsted-Lowry base; the Lewis base donates an electron pair.
Swapping donor and acceptor between acid and base.

Reading the words multiple bonds as one test for both lists. CO₂ and SO₂ are Lewis acids and CO and NO are Lewis bases. What decides is whether the molecule has a lone pair to GIVE or a place to TAKE one.
steps.memory_tip: Base gives the pair. NH₃, H₂O, CO and NO all carry a lone pair to give; the multiple bond is not what makes CO and NO bases.
steps.margin_note: Definition plus the three types with examples. For type (c), say that CO and NO donate a lone pair on the carbon or the nitrogen atom.

steps.label: Neutralisation
lines: Neutralisation in this theory is the
formation of a coordinate covalent bond
between the base and the acid.
(the oxygen atom donates its lone pair
to H⁺)

lines.text: Lewis acid = lone-pair acceptor; Lewis base = lone-pair donor

steps.why: The two definitions meet in the bond: the base's lone pair becomes the shared pair of a coordinate covalent bond, and that bond formation is what the theory calls neutralisation. Two errors are common in this step of the 4-mark answer: describing neutralisation as acid + base giving salt + water, which belongs to the older theories, and writing the example without naming which species donates the pair.
common_mistakes: Mixing the theories. In the Lewis theory the acid accepts a lone pair and the base donates one; proton donor and proton acceptor belong to Brønsted-Lowry.
Naming a species without saying which side it is on. Say plainly whether it accepts the lone pair (acid) or donates it (base).
steps.memory_tip: Neutralisation = one new coordinate bond. The base's lone pair becomes the shared pair.
steps.margin_note: Close with the boxed acceptor/donor pair — the two definitions side by side.

insider_note: This content is asked at two lengths — the unstarred 2-mark form asks only for the acid definition with BF₃, while the three-star 4-mark form is marked type by type, with the coordinate-bond neutralisation as the closing mark.
